newsitem.title: INDIA: India deputies grill government on Bofors scandal.
newsitem.headline: India deputies grill government on Bofors scandal.

text.p: A newspaper report naming former Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi as the main accused in a long-running corruption scandal linked to Swedish armsmaker Bofors AB caused an uproar in India's parliament on Wednesday.

The Indian Express newspaper said a proposed chargesheet by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) named Gandhi, who was assassinated in 1991, as the main conspirator in a kickback scam tied to a $1.3 billion artillery deal between India and Bofors.
The newspaper said the CBI had sent the chargesheet to the government for approval before filing charges through the courts in the 11-year-old scandal.
Rajiv Gandhi had all along denied any involvement, as did his family.
"The report has been submitted," a CBI official told Reuters, speaking anonymously. He refused to give other details.
Lawmakers charged the federal police with selectively leaking information on the probe into the artillery deal and asked the government to reveal the content of investigations into the Bofors case.
"If the investigations are complete, the house has a right to know," Congress party deputy Priya Ranjan Das Munshi said in the lower house, or Lok Sabha.
Das Munshi charged CBI director general Joginder Singh of passing information to the media.
House speaker P.A. Sangma was considering whether the right of lawmakers to information before it is made public had been violated, said Rita Verma, who was in the chair in Sangma's absence.

"Our stand is that the government must make a statement on it," Sushma Swaraj of the main opposition Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) told reporters. "If the CBI has completed its investigations, the House must be informed first."
"We must unearth the truth," said Sharad Yadav, a leader of Prime Minister Inder Kumar's Gujral's Janata Dal party.
The daily said the chargesheet also names other people, including a former minister and top bureaucrats, whom the CBI sought to prosecute.

The chargesheet had been sent to the government for formal clearance, the daily quoted sources in the cabinet as saying. Under Indian law, the CBI must have government approval before proceeding with prosecutions, even of former civil servants.
Once a chargesheet is formally approved, the CBI can file a regular chargesheet in the courts.
The newspaper said the CBI report alleged that Gandhi conspired to cause willful loss to the state exchequer and to allow middlemen a cut in the deal to buy howitzers from Bofors.
The CBI probe also said it failed to prove that Gandhi had benefited financially from the deal, the newspaper said.
Swiss police say there is evidence that Bofors paid about $40 million into various bank accounts in Switzerland during the time the contract with India was drawn up and settled.
The CBI has already named Italian businessman Ottavio Quattrocchi and his wife, Maria, as recipients of illegal payments made by Bofors.

Quattrocchi was the New Delhi representative of Italian engineering firm Snamprogetti Spa when India signed the deal with Bofors. He now lives in Malaysia. He and Snamprogetti have both denied any involvement in the alleged payments.
India has asked Malaysia to arrest and extradite Quattrocchi and his wife.
